newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean papers tip university dean as new premier.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean papers tip university dean as new premier.

text.p: South Korean newspapers predicted President Kim Young-sam would appoint a new prime minister on Monday, and tipped a university president with extensive cabinet experience as his top choice.
Leading dailies on Monday unanimously picked Koh Kun, 59, president of Seoul's Myungji University, as the most likely candidate to succeed Lee Soo-sung.
Kim has launched a sweeping reshuffle of his administration aimed at restoring his reputation badly tarnished by a scandal involving loans to failed Hanbo Steel Co.
Last Friday he replaced his chief secretary and three other top aides at the presidential Blue House.
An extensive reshuffle of cabinet positions, including the key finance ministry job, is widely expected after Kim names a new prime minister.
A Blue House official on Monday declined to comment on speculation over a new premier.
Newspapers said an announcement would be made on Monday afternoon. Yonhap Television News said it was more likely to come on Tuesday.
South Korean media have a checkered record of predicting cabinet changes.
Current prime minister Lee, an eminent legal scholar, was plucked from the presidency of Seoul National University by Kim in 1995.
Kim apologised last Tuesday over a loans-for-kickbacks scandal at Hanbo, which went bankrupt on January 23 after piling up debts of $5.8 billion.

Koh served as mayor of Seoul from 1988-1990 during the presidency of Roh Tae-woo. He was minister of home affairs, transportation, agriculture and forestry under the previous administration of Chun Doo Hwan during the early 1980s.
He took up his university post in 1994.

Koh was born in Seoul, but unusual for a high-flying establishment figure has worked extensively in southwest Cholla province, a traditional hotbed of opposition politics, and has come to be identified with Cholla.

Cholla residents believe their poor province has been deliberately deprived as punishment for opposition to central government, whose leaders are overwhelmingly from wealthy Kyongsang province next door.
Koh was governor of South Cholla province in 1979.
